title: BENJAMIN TOOK WIVES FROM DANCING WOMEN: WHY IS THIS STORY IN JUDGES?
paragraphs:
BENJAMIN TOOK WIVES FROM DANCING WOMEN: WHY IS THIS STORY IN JUDGES?
They hid in the vineyards. They watched the women dance. Then they took them. And somehow, this horrifying story became the final chapter of Judges. The question is not merely, “Why did God allow this story into the Bible?” The deeper question is whether we recognize the same human disease that made such a story possible—and whether we understand why we desperately need a King who can save us from ourselves.
There are passages in Scripture that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you sit there in silence and whisper...
“What did I just read?”
Judges 21 is one of them.

Israel has descended into chaos. A woman has already been horrifically abused and killed. A civil war has erupted. Thousands are dead. The tribe of Benjamin has nearly been annihilated. Israel has made reckless vows before God, and instead of humbly confronting the foolishness and sin that brought them to this point, they begin trying to solve one catastrophe by creating another.
Then comes one of the strangest scenes in the Old Testament.
The remaining Benjamite men are told to hide among the vineyards near Shiloh and wait for young women to come out to dance.
Then:

“Go and lie in wait in the vineyards, and watch; and behold, if the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come ye out of the vineyards, and catch you every man his wife of the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.”
—Judges 21:21, KJV
Read that again.
Hide.
Watch.
Wait.
Then take a wife.
What are we supposed to do with that?
Was God commanding this?
Was Scripture approving it?
Were these women willing?
Why would something this disturbing be preserved in the Bible?
And perhaps most importantly...
Where is Jesus in a story like this?
Because if we misunderstand why Judges records these events, we can make one of the most dangerous mistakes possible when reading Scripture:
We can confuse what the Bible describes with what God prescribes.
The Hebrew makes the disturbing nature of the scene difficult to soften.
The men are instructed:
וַחֲטַפְתֶּם לָכֶם אִישׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ
waḥăṭaptem lāḵem ʾîš ʾištô
The crucial verb comes from חָטַף (ḥāṭap), carrying the idea of seizing, snatching, or taking away.
This isn't romantic language.
This isn't the language of a wedding proposal beneath the stars.
The women of Shiloh were participating in a festival when the surviving Benjamites were instructed to seize wives from among them.
Whatever questions remain about details the narrative does not tell us, the text itself gives us no reason to turn this episode into a sentimental love story.
But there is something equally important we must understand.
The fact that an event appears in Scripture does not mean God approves of the event.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
Abraham lies.
Jacob deceives.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies Christ.
The disciples argue over greatness.
Scripture doesn't protect its heroes with public-relations departments.
It exposes them.
And Judges may be one of the clearest examples.
To understand chapter 21, you have to feel what has happened before it.
Judges begins after Joshua's generation passes away. Israel repeatedly abandons the LORD, suffers the consequences of rebellion, cries out, and receives deliverance.
But something happens as the book progresses.
The stories become darker.
The deliverers become increasingly compromised.
The nation's spiritual condition deteriorates.
By the final chapters, Israel is no longer simply being oppressed by enemies outside its borders.
Israel is destroying itself.
That is the horror.
Sin has moved from the gates...
into the house.
Judges 19 contains one of Scripture's most horrific accounts: the abuse and death of the Levite's concubine in Gibeah, a Benjaminite city.
Israel responds with war against Benjamin.
But righteous outrage becomes entangled with vengeance, rash vows, devastation, and further moral catastrophe.
Benjamin is almost wiped out.
Then Israel realizes what has happened.
An entire tribe may disappear.
The people weep.
But there is a terrible irony here.
They mourn the consequences while continuing to operate with the same broken moral reasoning that helped produce them.
They have sworn not to give their daughters as wives to Benjamin.
So they search for a loophole.
First comes Jabesh-gilead.

Because no one from that city had joined Israel's assembly, Israel attacks it. Men, married women, and others are killed, while four hundred young virgins are spared and given to Benjamin's survivors.
Still not enough.
Two hundred Benjamite men remain without wives.
And then someone develops another solution.
There is a festival at Shiloh.
Women will come out to dance.
Hide in the vineyards.
Take them.
Then, if their fathers or brothers object, Israel's leaders will intervene.
Do you see what is happening?
Human beings are attempting to repair the consequences of sin while refusing to escape the logic of sin.
One wound is covered by creating another wound.
One terrible decision requires another terrible decision.
A vow becomes a loophole.
A loophole becomes violence.
Violence becomes justification.
And everybody somehow keeps moving forward.
Until Scripture drops the final sentence.
Not merely the final sentence of the chapter.
The final sentence of the entire book.
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
—Judges 21:25, KJV
That sentence changes how you read everything that came before it.
The Hebrew is devastating:
אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
ʾên meleḵ bəyiśrāʾēl; ʾîš hayyāšār bəʿênāw yaʿăśeh.
“There was no king in Israel; each man would do what was right in his own eyes.”
Notice the tragedy.
They weren't necessarily walking around saying,
“I choose evil because evil is wonderful.”
They were doing what seemed right in their own eyes.
That is far more frightening.
Because some of humanity's darkest decisions are made by people who have already developed reasons for believing their decisions are justified.
That is Judges.
And if we're willing to be painfully honest...
sometimes that is us.
We sin.
Consequences come.
Then instead of running to God in genuine repentance, we start managing appearances.
We hide something.
Explain something.
Blame someone.
Rename something.
Find a loophole.
Create another compromise to protect the first compromise.
Then another.
And eventually we are standing inside a life we barely recognize, wondering how we got there.
It rarely happened in one enormous step.
It happened through hundreds of smaller moments when what seemed right in our eyes became more authoritative than what God had said.
That is why Judges 21 is not some embarrassing biblical relic that Christians need to hide from.
We need it.
We need Scripture to show us what humanity looks like when everyone becomes his own final moral authority.
And we need to be careful here.
Judges 21 does not say that every detail of Israel's behavior was commanded by God.
It does not tell us that God instructed the Benjamites to seize the dancing women.
It does not present their scheme as a timeless model for marriage.
It records what Israel did in a book deliberately portraying Israel's moral and spiritual collapse.
And then the narrator closes the entire book by telling us the spiritual atmosphere in which these things happened:
Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
The chapter therefore isn't teaching men how to find wives.
It is showing us how desperately Israel needed righteous rule.
Yet even saying, “Israel needed a king,” does not complete the biblical story.
Because eventually Israel got human kings.
Some were faithful in significant ways.
Many were not.
Even David—the great king whose dynasty becomes central to biblical hope—was a sinner who desperately needed mercy himself.
So the ache running through Judges ultimately reaches farther than Saul.
Farther than David.
Farther than Solomon.
Humanity needed something greater than another fallen man sitting on a throne.
We needed the King.
And centuries later, another word appears in Scripture:
βασιλεὺς
basileus.
King.
Jesus stands before Pilate, and the question of kingship hangs over the scene.
Jesus says:
“My kingdom is not of this world...”
—John 18:36, KJV
Then the innocent King is crucified.
Think about the reversal.
In Judges, human beings do what is right in their own eyes and others suffer because of it.
At Calvary, humanity does what is right in its own eyes...
and Jesus suffers because of it.
We condemn the innocent One.
We crown Him with thorns.
We mock Him.
We crucify Him.
Human rebellion reaches toward the Son of God.
And instead of answering sinners with the destruction we deserve, Christ gives His life to redeem sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin doesn't matter.
Grace is not God pretending evil is harmless.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
Yet God's love is so astonishing that the Son willingly came to save His enemies.
The Greek New Testament uses a beautiful word for redemption:
ἀπολύτρωσις
apolytrōsis.
Redemption.
Release secured through a ransom.
Paul writes that in Christ:
—Ephesians 1:7, KJV
That is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you've never hidden beside a vineyard.
But perhaps you've hidden something else.
A browser history.
An affair.
An addiction.
Bitterness.
Pride.
A secret relationship.
A private compromise.
A lie everyone believes.
A wound you turned into an excuse to wound other people.
Maybe you became skilled at constructing explanations for something your conscience once recognized immediately.
Maybe your favorite sentence became:
“God understands.”
Yes.
God understands more completely than we do.
And that should make us tremble before it makes us comfortable.
He understands the motive.
The excuse.
The wound beneath the behavior.
The person you blamed.
The night nobody saw.
The thought you never said aloud.
He understands everything.
And still...
He calls sinners to come.
Not to hide.
Not to negotiate.
Not to manufacture another loophole.
To repent.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια—metanoia—a turning, a change of mind that expresses itself in a redirected life.
Jesus did not come merely to make guilty people feel slightly better about themselves.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile.
To transform.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin wasn't really that serious.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
Your sin was serious enough for Christ to die...
and His grace is powerful enough to forgive the repentant sinner.
This is why the theme running from scandal to grace matters so much.
Scripture contains scandals because Scripture tells the truth about humanity.
But scandal doesn't get the final word.
Grace does.
Benjamin's story didn't end with complete annihilation.
Israel's story didn't end in Judges.
David's failure wasn't the end.
Peter's denial wasn't the end.
Paul's persecution of Christians wasn't the end.
And if you belong to Christ, your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
Jesus does.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean victims' suffering becomes insignificant.
It does not mean repentance is merely saying sorry and continuing unchanged.
Biblical grace never requires us to call darkness light.
Grace brings darkness into the light.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace confesses.
Grace repents.
Grace receives forgiveness that could never be earned.
Grace begins rebuilding what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe that's why this strange chapter survived thousands of years to reach you today.
Not because God wanted you to imitate the men hiding in the vineyards.
But because God wanted His people to see where life leads when everyone becomes king.
And maybe you have been sitting on that throne.
Determining truth according to your desires.
Defining obedience according to convenience.
Calling surrender “extreme.”
Calling compromise “freedom.”
Calling conviction “judgment.”
Calling delay “waiting for the right time.”
But there is already a King.
His name is Jesus.
And unlike the broken rulers of this world, He does not exploit His people for His own survival.
He gave Himself for theirs.
The King wore thorns.
The King carried the cross.
The King received the nails.
The King entered death.
And the King rose again.
That is Christianity.
Not broken people pretending they have never been broken.
Redeemed people confessing that Jesus Christ is greater than their ruin.
So perhaps the question isn't only:
“Why is this disturbing story in Judges?”
Perhaps another question has been waiting beneath it.
What have I been doing because it seemed right in my own eyes?
Let it find you.
What are you defending that God has been asking you to surrender?
What are you hiding that needs light?
Who have you hurt while convincing yourself you were justified?
What compromise started small but now owns more of your heart than you ever intended to give it?
Where have you been asking Jesus to be Savior while quietly refusing Him as King?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
You don't owe strangers the details of your private sins. But you can make a simple confession of dependence on Christ.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy your life, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to make another wounded person realize that repentance is not the end of hope.
It's where grace meets us.
Not because every line is easy to read.

Supporting Gospel work can be one genuine way of stewarding resources for God's glory when it is done freely, wisely, and cheerfully—not from guilt or coercion. Scripture teaches that Christian giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
A ministry cannot save you.
A Christian library cannot save you.
A comment cannot save you.
Sharing an article cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
The deepest call of this article is not “support us.”
It is:
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding.
Lay down the crown you've been wearing in your own heart.
There is a King.
And astonishingly, the King who has every right to judge sinners stretched out His hands to save them.
Judges ends with humanity doing what is right in its own eyes.
The Gospel brings us to Jesus and teaches us to finally lift our eyes to Him.
Because perhaps the most terrifying place you can live is a kingdom where you are your own king...
and the most beautiful moment of your life may be the moment you finally surrender the throne.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but grace decides who you can become after you meet the King there.
